newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: RUGBY UNION-PROFESSIONAL REFEREES NEEDED, SAYS MCINTOSH.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-PROFESSIONAL REFEREES NEEDED, SAYS MCINTOSH.

text.p: Inconsistent refereeing in rugby's Super 12 competition has forced Natal provincial coach Ian McIntosh to echo the plea he made last year for a professional refereeing panel to handle all games.

Before last year's Super 12 semifinals, McIntosh said it was crucial referees and coaches from South Africa, New Zealand and Australia were on the same wavelength throughout the southern hemisphere series.

So far this has not happened during the 1997 Super 12. Although a referees conference was held in Sydney in February to try to achieve some uniformity, none of the provincial or state rugby coaches was involved.
This year's competition is almost halfway through and has been beset by complaints from coaches of teams playing away from home directed at harmful - and inconsistent - refereeing.
Seeing no other alternative, Australian Rugby Football Union chief executive officer John O'Neill earlier this week called for neutral referees to be appointed.
"The inconsistencies, the different interpretations of referees in each country, are still there. We've just got to wear the coat of neutral referees," he said.

But McIntosh disagrees: "The answer is not neutral referees but a professional panel of refs. Then, once everyone is playing to the same pattern, you can't complain when the ref blows and you're nailed.
McIntosh believes the main problem to be addressed is the different approach by players from the three countries at the point of breakdown.

"In New Zealand, and to a similar extent in Australia, you're allowed to hold on to the ball a little longer after a tackle to allow players to cover. Also, you can come in from the side of the maul and play the ball a lot more on the ground than we do in South Africa.
"Here in South Africa, we are strict to the law and have to release the ball in the tackle," McIntosh said.
"I happen to believe the New Zealand approach is the best as it keeps the game flowing - but it can only flow if both teams and the referee follow that same approach."
